question:
Let $f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1$.

(a) Find all local maxima and minima.

(b) Prove whether $f$ is strictly increasing/decreasing in any interval and relate this to the solution set of $f'(x) > 0$.

(c) Consider $g(x) = f(x) + a$ for some constant $a$. If $a$ is chosen such that $g(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=1$, find the required value of $a$ and verify your answer.
explanation:
**Concepts tested:** Application of derivatives, critical points, increasing/decreasing functions, use of first and second derivative tests, effect of shifting functions.

(a) $f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1$
First derivative:
$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3$
Set $f'(x) = 0$:
$3x^2 - 3 = 0 \implies x^2 = 1 \implies x = 1, -1$

Second derivative:
$f''(x) = 6x$
At $x=1$, $f''(1) = 6 > 0$ so $x=1$ is a local minimum.
At $x=-1$, $f''(-1) = -6 < 0$ so $x=-1$ is a local maximum.

Max at $x=-1$; min at $x=1$.

(b) For $f$ to be strictly increasing:
$f'(x) > 0 \implies 3x^2 - 3 > 0 \implies x^2 > 1 \implies x > 1$ or $x < -1$
So $f$ is strictly increasing for $(-\infty, -1)$ and $(1, \infty)$, strictly decreasing for $(-1, 1)$.
Thus, the behaviour of $f$ is governed by the sign of $f'(x)$.

(c) $g(x) = f(x) + a = x^3 - 3x + 1 + a$
To have a local minimum at $x=1$:
$g'(x) = f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3$. At $x=1$, $g'(1) = 0$ (already holds).
Now check $g''(x) = f''(x) = 6x$, $g''(1) = 6 > 0$; so $x=1$ is a local minimum for any $a$.
But the value of $a$ does not affect the position of the minimum, only its height. So $a$ can be any real number, and $g(x)$ will always have a local minimum at $x=1$ if $x=1$ is a stationary point.
To verify, $g'(1) = 0$ and $g''(1) = 6 > 0$. Yes, $x=1$ is a minimum for any $a$.

options.A:
(a) Local maximum at $x=1$ and local minimum at $x=-1$
(b) $f$ is increasing on $(-1,1)$ and decreasing on $(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty)$
(c) Required value is $a=0$ only
options.B:
(a) Local maximum at $x=-1$ and local minimum at $x=1$
(b) $f$ is strictly increasing on $(-\infty,-1)$ and $(1,\infty)$, and strictly decreasing on $(-1,1)$
(c) $a$ can be any real number because vertical shifting does not change the position of the local minimum
options.C:
(a) Local maxima occur at both $x=-1$ and $x=1$
(b) $f$ is strictly increasing for all real $x$
(c) Required value is $a=-1$
options.D:
(a) There are no local maxima or minima
(b) $f'(x)>0$ has no solution
(c) No value of $a$ can make $x=1$ a local minimum
